note: The reference survey on benchmark contamination, the reason published model scores cannot be taken at face value.
title: Benchmark Data Contamination of Large Language Models: A Survey
explain_beginner: AI companies often boast that their models score extremely high on standard tests of reasoning, coding, or knowledge. But there is a hidden problem: many of these test questions, along with their correct answers, may already exist somewhere on the internet and could have been swept up into the enormous piles of text used to train the model. If that happens, a model is not really solving the problem, it is remembering the answer it saw during training, similar to a student who saw the exam questions in advance. This paper is a survey that pulls together everything researchers currently know about this issue, sometimes called benchmark contamination. It explains the different ways contamination can creep in, from a model seeing the exact test with its answers, to more subtle cases where it only saw similar material on the same topic. It also describes ways researchers try to detect and reduce this problem, while being honest that no current fix removes the risk entirely. The upshot is that headline AI test scores deserve a healthy dose of doubt.
explain_business: If you are evaluating AI vendors based on their published benchmark scores for coding, reasoning, or knowledge tasks, this survey is a reason for caution. A high score on a popular public benchmark does not guarantee the model will perform that well on genuinely new problems, because the model may have already seen versions of the test during training. Reported contamination levels varying from roughly 1 to 45 percent across different models and benchmarks means the size of this risk differs a lot depending on which model and which test you are looking at, so no blanket assumption is safe. Practically, this argues for testing vendor claims against your own private, non-public tasks rather than trusting a leaderboard number alone, and for favoring benchmarks that are refreshed regularly or built after a model's training cutoff. There is no fix a business can simply buy here. Detection and cleanup methods described in the paper are still research-stage, imperfect, and computationally expensive, so the safest posture for now is treating public benchmark scores as an upper bound rather than a guarantee.
explain_practitioner: This survey organizes benchmark data contamination into four levels: label-level (a model sees test questions with their correct answers), data-level (test content without labels), information-level (metadata like time or label distributions), and semantic-level (material on the same topic or from the same source, without literal overlap). It reviews detection methods including simple text-overlap checks (GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap, GPT-4 used 50-character overlap), membership inference, perplexity-based tests, and chronological comparisons that track performance drops on problems published after a model's training cutoff. Mitigation approaches covered include dynamic benchmarks refreshed over time such as LiveCodeBench, rewriting existing questions (EvoEval reports a meaningful accuracy drop on HumanEval once questions are reworded), and private or encrypted test sets. Reported contamination rates across fifteen models studied ranged from about 1 percent to 45 percent depending on the benchmark. A limitation the authors state plainly is that even paraphrased or reworded test data can still leak semantic information, and one study showed a training technique could raise benchmark scores by up to 15 percent while evading standard contamination detectors.
